label: Learning to ride a bike

what_happens.title: How learning to ride works
goals: Riding is balance, pedalling and steering
It is learned step by step
Wobbles and falls are part of learning
what_happens.parentSkill: Explain the three skills: balance, pedal, steer, and that you learn them one at a time.

who_is_there.title: Who helps me learn
who_is_there.parentSkill: Agree exactly how you will help: holding the back of the seat or the shoulders, and when you will let go.

what_i_do.title: What I do on the bike
goals: Brake to stop and put feet down
If I fall, check, rest, try again
what_i_do.parentSkill: Practise braking first, so your child knows how to stop before going faster.

if_scared.title: If I am scared of falling
goals: Falling can happen and usually means small scrapes
Wobbling is normal and gets better
Calm tools: helmet, slow breaths, going at my speed
if_scared.parentSkill: Name the fear honestly: 'You might fall. The helmet protects your head, and scrapes get better.'

rehearsal.title: Let's get ready to ride
goals: Practise the stop: brake, feet down
rehearsal.parentSkill: Let your child practise putting on and clicking the helmet themselves, and squeezing the brakes while you push the bike.

steps: Put on a helmet and click the strap
Find a flat, quiet place like a park path
Sit on the seat with feet touching the ground
Push the pedals while a grown-up runs alongside
Look ahead, steer and squeeze the brakes to stop
Rest, drink water and try again
sensory: a helmet strap clicking under the chin
a wobbly feeling in the handlebars
a bump on the knee or the hands
a fast heartbeat when going faster
honestyNotes: Falling is part of learning to ride and can cause scrapes and bumps; never promise no falls. A grown-up holding the bike will let go at some point; agree when, never trick the child. Always a helmet. Let the parent decide balance bike, training wheels or pedals.

fallbackAnswer: Falling can happen when learning, and it can make a scrape or a bump that stings.
The helmet protects your head, and scrapes get better.
[[GROWNUP]] will hold on until you say, let go.
You decide the signal together.

questionButtons.text: Why do I wear a helmet?
fallbackAnswer: A helmet protects your head if you fall.
Every rider wears one, even grown-ups.
Wobbling happens while your body learns to balance.
It gets better with practice, and going a bit faster helps.
Squeeze the brakes on the handlebars and put your feet down.
We can practise stopping first.
Lots of kids are learning too.
Everyone wobbled when they started.

questionButtons.text: What if I go too fast?
fallbackAnswer: Squeeze the brakes gently to slow down.
We practise on a flat path where it is easy to stop.
We practise in a quiet place with no cars, like a park path.
Roads come much later, with a grown-up.
Bikes make whirring and clicking sounds when the wheels turn.
That is the chain and the wheels doing their job.

questionButtons.text: What if I can't do it?
fallbackAnswer: Most kids need a few tries on different days.
[[GROWNUP]] is proud of you for trying every time.

questionButtons.text: Who else is on the path?
fallbackAnswer: Walkers, runners and other riders.
We keep to one side and say, excuse me.

techniques.label: Helmet click
techniques.how: Let your child put on and click the helmet themselves.

techniques.label: Gliding first
techniques.how: Glide with feet off the ground before pedalling.

techniques.label: Brakes first
techniques.how: Practise squeezing the brakes before going faster.

techniques.label: A let-go signal
techniques.how: Agree that you let go only when your child says so.

techniques.label: Look ahead
techniques.how: Pick a tree or a bench to look at while riding.

techniques.label: A little first aid kit
techniques.how: Bring water, wipes and fun bandages.

techniques.label: Short sessions
techniques.how: Ride for short times with breaks.

techniques.label: Path manners
techniques.how: Keep to one side and say, excuse me.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

pain: A scrape stings, and then it gets better. Let's clean it.
body: Your body is learning to balance.
sensory: The wind feels nice on your face.
The clicking is just the chain.
strangers: Other people share the path. Keep to one side.
separation: I'll hold on until you say, let go.
I'm right here running next to you.
safety: Squeeze the brakes to slow down.
social: Lots of kids are learning too.
love: I'm proud of you for trying again.

Hazel got a shiny red bike.
First Hazel put on a helmet with a strap, click.
Then Grandpa Hedgehog took her to the flat path by the pond.

She got up and tried again.

Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.

Balance on a bike comes from forward motion; the faster the wheels turn, the steadier the bike feels.
That is why going a little faster often makes it easier, not harder.
Steering and looking ahead keep the bike pointed where the rider wants to go.
Most kids need several sessions before it clicks.
[[CHILD]] can count how many pedal strokes they manage each session.
Agreeing a signal for letting go builds trust; tricking a rider usually makes the next try harder.
Path etiquette matters: ride on the right side, ring a bell or call out when passing.
Some kids learn faster on a balance bike or with pedals removed first.
Watching another kid ride can make the skill click.
[[CHILD]] can teach a younger kid later, once it clicks.
Starting with one pedal at the top position gives the strongest first push.
Looking far ahead makes small wobbles correct themselves.
Using both brakes evenly gives the smoothest stop.
Short sessions with breaks work better than one long, tired session.
[[CHILD]] can set a goal, like riding from one bench to the next.
Fear of falling is useful; it makes riders careful, and it shrinks as skill grows.
Most learning falls are slow and low, causing scrapes rather than serious injuries.
Gloves and knee pads can make a nervous rider feel braver.
Practising on grass makes falls softer, though pedalling is harder.
[[CHILD]] can decide how long each session lasts.
Checking the bike before riding, tyres, brakes and seat height, is what experienced riders do.
The seat should let feet touch the ground for beginners.
Choosing a quiet, flat place makes the first session a success.
Having water and a snack keeps energy up.
[[CHILD]] can be in charge of the pre-ride check.
